docs.title: 1.1 Documented Reference Capabilities
docs.text:
• GitHub Spec Kit (github/spec-kit, github.github.com/spec-kit/, read 20 Nov 2026):
  • Constitution as Root Anchor: .specify/memory/constitution.md sets project guidelines, principles, and architectural rules against which subsequent specs are evaluated. Crucially, the constitution is amendable and versioned (containing formal amendment procedures, version increments, and sync impact analysis), providing a stable yet evolving governance baseline.
  • Spec-Driven Development (SDD): Clear separation between what to build (spec.md user scenarios and requirements) and how to build (plan.md technical architecture).
  • Checklists as "Unit Tests of Requirements": templates/commands/checklist.md evaluates specification clarity, completeness, and consistency before any code is generated.
  • Idea Assessment Lifecycle: Structured 5-stage gating (intake \(\to\) research \(\to\) define \(\to\) shape \(\to\) decide) outputting evidence-backed go, needs-clarification, or kill recommendations.
  • Extensible Layering: Presets, overlays, and local overrides that modify templates without forking core logic.
  • Builderpack (builderpack.com/docs, builderpack.com/actions, read 20 Nov 2026):
  • Dual-Modality Capability Units: Modular actions that function interchangeably as deterministic workflow automation steps or autonomous agent-callable tools within HubSpot.
  • Typed Parameter Contracts: Explicit input definitions (literal strings, CRM property tokens, prior step outputs) with fixed-choice enumerations and required/optional constraints.
  • Asynchronous Processing: Structured execution pattern where background research operations resolve cleanly without stalling orchestration threads.
  • Explicit Output Tokens: Granular output schemas mapped directly into subsequent execution nodes or state variables.

docs.title: 1.2 Proposed Factory Synthesis
docs.text: The Factory synthesizes these two paradigms into an integrated agent authoring lifecycle: * It applies Spec Kit's specification rigor to agent definition: extracting explicit data boundaries, prohibited actions, and observable acceptance criteria before prompting or coding begins. * It applies Builderpack's capability contract to tool design: treating every agent capability as an isolated, typed, and permission-bounded block that declares its dependencies, error behaviors, and data flow. * It binds them together with an auditable evidence manifest that distinguishes generated assets from executed, verified outcomes.

docs.title: 1.3 Reference Characteristics NOT Inherited (Boundary Distinctions)
docs.text: Reference Characteristic Why the Factory Distinguishes / Does Not Inherit It Spec Kit: Repository Workflow Focus Spec Kit's reference workflows and templates focus on software engineering features in Git repositories. The Factory adapts its specification discipline specifically to agent systems—defining prompt boundaries, model-context limits, non-deterministic reasoning loops, tool permissions, and adversarial guardrails. Spec Kit: Checklist Conflation In Spec Kit, passing a requirements.md checklist verifies that requirements are well-written and consistent. The Factory treats requirement consistency as a check on specification quality, never as proof of functional agent execution or formal verification. Builderpack: HubSpot Platform Coupling Builderpack's public documentation describes an action pack configured specifically for HubSpot portals (OAuth, CRM properties, Professional/Enterprise tiers). The Factory defines provider- and platform-agnostic capability contracts, defaulting to no specific CRM or vendor runtime. Builderpack: Action Catalog vs. Factory Lifecycle Builderpack provides a curated catalog of pre-built actions for HubSpot; its public docs do not establish whether it includes standalone evaluation suites or adversarial guardrails, nor do they establish an open tool marketplace. The Factory focuses on the tooling lifecycle—authoring, evaluating, packaging, and revising arbitrary agent capabilities with explicit failure modes and auditable evidence.

docs.title: 2. The End-to-End Factory Journey
docs.text:
The Factory lifecycle transitions an ambiguous concept into a verified, inspectable agent pack through six disciplined stages:

flowchart TD
    S1["1. Idea Intake"] --> S2["2. Clarification"]
    S2 --> S3["3. Specification Contract"]
    S3 --> S4["4. Inspectable Agent Pack"]
    S4 --> S5["5. Supervised Evaluation & Evidence Review"]
    S5 <--> S6["6. Revision & Invalidation"]

docs.title: Stage 1: Idea Intake
docs.text:
• Input: Raw, unstructured natural-language brief, business pain point, operational sketch, or napkin idea.
  • Output Artifact: idea_intake.md (captured raw intent, requester identity, proposed domain, and initial stated goals).
  • Decision Owner: Agent Requester / Sponsor.
  • Observable Acceptance Criterion: Complete text capture without algorithmic distortion; the Factory acknowledges raw input without silently rewriting, assuming technical constraints, or committing to feasibility.

docs.title: Stage 2: Clarification
docs.text:
• Input: idea_intake.md.
  • Output Artifact: clarification_record.md structured into:
  • [CONFIRMED REQUIREMENTS]: Articulated, non-conflicting bounds.
  • [PROPOSED DEFAULTS]: Explicitly highlighted structural defaults suggested by the Factory.
  • [CONSEQUENTIAL AMBIGUITIES]: Explicit inquiries where business logic, permissions, or escalation thresholds conflict or require clarification.
  • Decision Owner: Agent Owner / Definer.
  • Observable Acceptance Criterion: The Factory surfaces consequential ambiguities (conflicting business rules, missing essential inputs, or ambiguous tool permissions) and presents explicit choices; it never silently invents default business policies, fallback credentials, or loose permissions.

docs.title: Stage 3: Specification Contract
docs.text:
• Input: Resolved clarification_record.md with explicit owner decisions.
  • Output Artifact: spec.md (The binding Requirements Contract) containing:
  • Functional goals and observable acceptance criteria.
  • Required tool contracts and external dependencies.
  • Explicit Prohibited Action List (hard operational boundaries).
  • Traceability Matrix: $\(\text{Requirement ID(s)} \longleftrightarrow \text{Acceptance Criteria} \longleftrightarrow \text{Planned Artifact(s)} \longleftrightarrow \text{Evidence Record}\)$
  • Decision Owner: Technical Planner / Solution Architect.
  • Observable Acceptance Criterion: Requirements link (via 1:1, 1:many, or many:many relationships as appropriate) to intended artifacts and observable validation checks. Unsupported integrations, missing external APIs, and contradictions are visibly flagged as unresolved blockers.

docs.title: Stage 4: Inspectable Agent Pack Compilation
docs.text:
• Input: Signed-Off spec.md.
  • Output Artifact: Agent Build Pack (filesystem bundle):
  • instructions.md: Core system instructions, cleanly separated into model-agnostic business rules vs. target-specific platform adapters.
  • tools/: Declarative capability contracts (OpenAPI 3.1 / JSON Schema / MCP definitions).
  • runtime/: Scaffolding entrypoints, setup documentation, environment requirements, and explicit platform dependencies.
  • tests/: Factory-generated edge-case and failure-mode test suites.
  • Decision Owner: Integration Developer / Automation Assembler.
  • Observable Acceptance Criterion: The package is generated as an inspectable filesystem bundle with syntactically valid static assets; core business behavior is structurally separated from platform adapter logic; universal compatibility is not claimed. Mandatory container boot is not a condition of generating or exporting a pack. Boot checks, static linting, functional evaluations, and adversarial probes are distinct forms of evidence, not equivalent passes. Evaluation remains strictly optional for pack export; an untested pack can be inspected and exported with a clear NOT RUN status on its evaluation dimensions, never with a claim that it works.

docs.title: Stage 5: Supervised Evaluation & Evidence Review
docs.text:
• Input: Compiled Agent Build Pack + Evaluation Configuration (scope, test cases, permissions, runtime parameters).
  • Factory Supervised-Evaluation Capability: A human supervisor:
  • Reviews and scopes the evaluation plan, test cases, tool permissions, mock bindings, and execution conditions prior to any run.
  • Can start, pause, stop, and inspect an evaluation run when separately authorized.
  • Reviews recorded outcomes, error traces, and boundary compliance before signing off.
  • Export Optionality: Evaluation is strictly optional for pack export. An un-evaluated or partially evaluated pack can be exported provided all unevaluated dimensions are clearly labeled NOT RUN.
  • Output Artifact: Proposed Evidence Record (audit_manifest.json): Detailed record linking evaluated assets, model/configuration, external dependencies, and environment to logged outcomes across distinct evidence dimensions.
  • Decision Owner: Evaluation Supervisor / Approver.
  • Observable Acceptance Criterion: Traceable alignment between claimed results and physical execution logs. Any observed unauthorized tool action, defined confidentiality breach, boundary-breaking injection, or false verification claim rejects that evaluated pack, regardless of overall scores.

docs.title: Stage 6: Revision & Invalidation
docs.text:
• Input: User feedback, modified requirements, newly discovered edge cases, or failing test traces.
  • Output Artifact: revision_delta.md (Versioned mutation record):
  • Textual diff of changed requirements.
  • State invalidation table: Records affected downstream code, adapters, and test evidence whose current applicability is updated to STALE / INVALIDATED.
  • Decision Owner: Joint: Agent Owner (for requirement changes) & Technical Planner (for spec updates).
  • Observable Acceptance Criterion: Historical results are preserved in the audit log (an earlier pass on version X remains on record as having passed version X); mutating an upstream requirement updates the current applicability status of affected downstream evidence to STALE / INVALIDATED relative to the new version Y. Acceptance criteria are never silently relaxed to force a passing score.

docs.title: 3. Reusable Capability Contract
docs.text:
Every tool, action, or integration block within an Agent Pack is governed by a declarative, machine-readable Capability Contract (capability_contract.json / tool_definition.json). It defaults to no specific CRM or vendor ecosystem.

classDiagram
    class CapabilityContract {
        +String capability_id
        +SemVer version
        +String purpose_and_intent
        +JSONSchema input_schema
        +JSONSchema output_schema
        +PermissionScope permissions
        +DataBoundaryRules data_boundaries
        +PlatformPrerequisites dependencies
        +FailureModeCatalog failure_modes
        +EvidenceStatus evidence_status
    }

docs.title: 3.1 Mandatory Contract Schema Fields
docs.text:
1. Identity & Purpose:
  2. capability_id: Unique canonical name (e.g., company_intelligence_lookup).
  3. version: Semantic version string (major.minor.patch).
  4. purpose_and_intent: Unambiguous description of what the tool accomplishes and when an agent should invoke it.
  5. Data Contracts:
  6. input_schema: Declarative schema (such as JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 or OpenAPI 3.1) defining all parameters, types, regex formats, fixed-choice enums, default values, and required fields.
  7. output_schema: Declarative schema defining terminal response properties, output tokens, and payload structures.
  8. Permissions & Execution Boundaries:
  9. permissions: Explicit permission flags (e.g., network_egress: true, filesystem_write: false, data_mutation: false).
  10. data_boundaries: Explicit data-handling constraints (e.g., prohibited PII passing, mandatory secret redaction, token masking rules).
  11. Platform & Runtime Dependencies:
  12. dependencies: Declared runtime prerequisites (e.g., required runtime version, network reachability, protocol support like MCP or HTTP REST).
  13. Failure Modes & Degradation Behaviors:
  14. failure_modes: Structured catalog of expected error conditions and mandatory recovery responses:
    • HTTP 429 / Rate Limit: Declares backoff expectation or graceful user notification.
    • HTTP 500 / Downstream Crash: Declares fallback payload or explicit failure message (prohibits hallucinating mock success).
    • Schema Mismatch / Malformed Output: Declares immediate validation rejection.
  15. Multi-Dimensional Evidence Status:
  16. evidence_status: Status record tracking creation, execution outcome, assumption confidence, and current applicability.

docs.title: 3.2 Visibility of Requirement-to-Capability Mismatches
docs.text: The Factory defines capability contracts as standalone, local specifications without defaulting to HubSpot integration or presuming a commercial marketplace. When an agent specification requires an action that conflicts with an available capability contract, the Factory surfaces the mismatch in the trace matrix: * Parameter Type Clash: If spec.md specifies an integer account ID but the capability schema requires an alphanumeric string, the compiler raises a SCHEMA_TYPE_MISMATCH blocker. * Permission Deficit: If the agent brief requires creating an external record but the capability contract declares data_mutation: false, the Factory flags a PERMISSION_BOUNDARY_VIOLATION. * Missing Error Handling: If the brief requires uninterrupted uptime but the capability declares unhandled 500 crashes, the Factory flags an UNMITIGATED_FAILURE_MODE.

docs.title: 4. Diverse Users & The Collaborative Backbone
docs.text:
The Factory provides a single, unified architectural backbone while accommodating differentiated guidance, technical depth, and handoff mechanisms across diverse user roles. One individual may hold several roles (e.g., a solo founder acting as requester, planner, and developer). The Factory does not select a developer-only audience, a specific workflow, or a single runtime.

docs.title: 5. Evidence & Change Governance Rules
docs.text: To ensure complete epistemic honesty and prevent deceptive completeness, the Factory operates under strict evidence and mutation invariants.

docs.title: 5.1 Multi-Dimensional Evidence Architecture
docs.text:
Rather than forcing all lifecycle information into a single mutually exclusive status tag, evidence is tracked across four distinct, complementary dimensions:

  1. Artifact Creation Status:
  2. GENERATED: The file, prompt, or test stub exists on disk.
  3. NOT CREATED: The artifact has not been authored or compiled.
  4. Check Execution & Outcome:
  5. NOT RUN: The check or validation case was defined, but was not executed in a runtime environment.
  6. EXECUTED-PASSED: The check was executed in an authorized environment and all assertions passed with logged stdout/stderr and exit code 0.
  7. EXECUTED-FAILED: The check was executed in an authorized environment and failed one or more assertions (raw failure trace retained).
  8. Assumption Confidence:
  9. VERIFIED: The dependency, credential format, or external behavior has been empirically confirmed via test or verified schema.
  10. UNVERIFIED ASSUMPTION: Any dependency, key format, runtime behavior, or environment prerequisite assumed by the Factory without empirical confirmation.
  11. Current Applicability (Temporal Relevance):
  12. CURRENT: The evidence directly applies to the active, unmodified version of the specification and pack.
  13. STALE / INVALIDATED: An upstream requirement or instruction has mutated since this check was performed, rendering the evidence historically valid for its original version but invalid for current applicability.

docs.title: 5.2 Preservation of Historical Results & Version Linkage
docs.text:
• Preservation of History: Prior test results are preserved as immutable historical facts. An earlier pass (EXECUTED-PASSED on version X) is never deleted or rewritten as though it never occurred; instead, its current applicability status is marked STALE / INVALIDATED relative to the newly modified version Y.
  • Proposed Evidence Record (audit_manifest.json): Every recorded check links to an auditable record identifying:
  • The exact pack snapshot and runtime entrypoint evaluated.
  • The specific test cases, assertions, and boundary probes executed.
  • Declared external dependencies and mock service bindings.
  • The model family, version, and runtime configuration evaluated.
  • The execution environment description and raw timestamped log traces.
  • Role of Hashes: Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) may be used to link records to exact file snapshots and detect drift; hashes link versions, but do not prove functional correctness or safety.

docs.title: 5.3 Auditable Evidence Standard & Bounded Claims
docs.text:
• All evidence is defined as auditable against physical log files, network capture dumps, and disk artifacts. Claims of evidence being "unforgeable" are explicitly rejected.
  • All claims regarding safety and performance are strictly bounded claims about observed results in finite test episodes. Passing a finite test suite does not constitute a universal guarantee against unobserved failures, nor does it guarantee the universal absence of violations.

docs.title: 5.4 Automatic Disqualification Invariants (Hard Failures)
docs.text: The following occurrences constitute non-negotiable rejection conditions (REJECT) for an evaluated pack, which cannot be offset, diluted, or forgiven by high aggregate scores on other benchmarks: 1. Observed Unauthorized Action: The agent attempts an action, tool call, or API invocation not explicitly permitted in its capability contract. 2. Observed Confidentiality Breach: The agent discloses internal secrets, unmasked PII, or data explicitly designated as confidential in spec.md. (Editable system prompts are not automatically assumed to be confidential; protection follows explicit confidentiality requirements defined in spec.md). 3. Observed Boundary-Breaking Injection: The agent complies with adversarial prompt injections, violating stated operational constraints. 4. False Verification Claim: Any artifact, manifest, or report claiming an assertion was tested or verified when no corresponding verifiable log trace exists.

docs.title: 6. Planning Governance Ledger
docs.text: This ledger records the formal status of product direction, working technical proposals, and unresolved owner choices. A model-authored ledger does not establish approval; only explicit owner decisions establish approved scope.

docs.title: 6.1 Confirmed Direction (Approved Scope Decisions)
docs.text:
• The Product is the Factory: All design effort focuses on the meta-tooling that clarifies, specifies, packages, evaluates, and revises agents. Downstream workflows (triage, extraction, routing) are benchmark test vectors, not the product definition.
  • Supervised Evaluation Capability in v1 (Newly Confirmed Scope): v1 must have the capability for supervised evaluation:
  • A human supervisor reviews the evaluation scope, test cases, permissions, mock bindings, and conditions.
  • A human supervisor can start, pause, stop, and inspect an evaluation run when separately authorized.
  • A human supervisor reviews recorded outcomes and boundary compliance.
  • Export Invariant: Evaluation is strictly optional for pack export. An un-evaluated or partially evaluated pack can be inspected and exported with clear NOT RUN labels, never with a claim that it works. Boot checks, static linting, and functional/security evaluations are different forms of evidence, not equivalent passes. Mandatory container boot is not a condition of generating or exporting a pack.
  • Specification Discipline: Every agent originates from an unambiguous, traceable requirements contract (spec.md).
  • Decoupled Architecture: Core business behavior is structurally separated from platform-specific adapters and declarative capability contracts.
  • Auditable Multi-Dimensional Evidence: Separation of creation, outcome, assumption, and applicability; preservation of historical results; automated invalidation of current applicability upon requirement mutations; zero tolerance for false verification claims.
  • Hard Disqualification Invariants: Safety violations, unauthorized actions, confidentiality breaches of designated data, and false claims trigger immediate rejection regardless of aggregate performance.
  • Multi-Role Collaborative Scope: Product accommodates defiers, assemblers, and approvers rather than forcing a single developer-only persona.

docs.title: 6.2 Proposed Technical Defaults (Working Hypotheses — Not Formally Approved)
docs.text: Note: The following items are working proposals and design concepts to explore; they remain subject to future architectural review and do not constitute approved owner commitments: * UI Views & Progressive Disclosure: Proposing a unified product with four progressive role views (Brief, Spec, Artifact, Evidence) rather than fragmented point tools. * Specific Handoff Mechanisms: Concepts such as Git-native branch reviews, visual parameter cards, white-labeled client delivery packs, compliance reports, and sandbox review views are exploratory proposals. * Schema Specifications: Proposing OpenAPI 3.1 / JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) as standard capability contract formats. * Containerized Execution Design: Proposing rootless, ephemeral containers with mock services and denied-by-default networking for future local test execution designs. * Cryptographic Version Linking: Proposing SHA-256 file hashing as an audit mechanism to link evidence records to version snapshots.

docs.title: 6.3 Unresolved Owner Choices (Explicitly Preserved for Future Decision)
docs.text:
1. Target Provider & Framework Prioritization: Prioritizing Anthropic Messages API vs. OpenAI Responses API vs. Google ADK vs. LangGraph or other runtimes remains an open planning decision.
  2. Primary Entry Persona Selection: Selecting which persona (Business Owner vs. Planner vs. Automation Specialist vs. Developer vs. Agency) will serve as the initial commercial wedge remains an open decision to be guided by customer discovery.
  3. Benchmark Workflow Selection: Choosing which specific workflow briefs (support triage, extraction, routing) will serve as the initial benchmark corpus for testing the Factory remains an open choice.

Boundary Notice: This document establishes the reconciled planning contract for the Agent Development Factory. It authorizes no implementation, candidate generation, code execution, environment setup, testing, spending, account connection, or deployment, and preserves the existing review block.

docs.title: Agent Development Factory: Persona Opportunity Map
docs.text:
Document Status: Product Planning Hypotheses (Not Validated Demand) Document Date: November 19, 2026 Audience: For Raja's Review Operational Invariant: The Factory remains the product. Sales, research, and extraction agents are possible generated outputs, not replacement product definitions. All persona definitions, fit evaluations, and design implications are hypotheses to be tested, not proven market facts.

[!IMPORTANT] GOVERNANCE & PLANNING INVARIANT This document establishes planning hypotheses and persona evaluation criteria only. It does not select a primary persona, nor does it authorize implementation, candidate generation, testing, environment creation, spending, deployment, or access to held builds and derivative materials.

docs.title: 1. Core Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Design for Multi-Role Collaboration: Model the Factory experience as a structured collaboration between the person who defines the agent (business intent/boundaries), the person who assembles or integrates it (tool schemas/runtime scaffolding), and the person who approves its organizational use (security/compliance/budget). Do not compress all three roles into a single hypothetical technical persona.
  2. Preserve Progressive Depth: Explore role-tailored entry points (e.g., guided brief interrogation for owners, specification review for planners, artifact inspection for builders, evidence review for approvers) as distinct views rather than fragmented, separate products.
  3. Avoid Premature Persona Selection: Do not lock into developer-first, business-first, or agency-first entry before validating recurring need, willingness to pay, tolerance for setup, and access to implementation resources.

docs.title: 2. Competitive Context: What Builderpack Actually Shows
docs.text:
• Primary Sources Examined (Read on Nov 19, 2026):
  • [1] Builderpack Home (https://www.builderpack.com/)
  • [2] Builderpack Actions Catalog (https://www.builderpack.com/actions)
  • [3] Builderpack Setup Documentation (https://www.builderpack.com/docs)
  • [4] Builderpack Use Cases (https://www.builderpack.com/use-cases)

docs.title: Verified Site Characteristics
docs.text:
• HubSpot-Centric Action Pack: Builderpack advertises a curated library of 19 actions focused on company research, social/web intelligence, content creation, and utility functions designed specifically for HubSpot environments.
  • Dual Execution Modality: The site describes these 19 actions as dual-purpose: they can execute either as standard HubSpot workflow automation steps or as agent-invokable tools.
  • Prerequisites & Installation: Requires an OAuth installation into an existing HubSpot portal (specifically requiring a Professional or Enterprise portal tier) with pre-mapped inputs and outputs.
  • Described Use Cases: Explicitly targeted at sales prospect research, competitive marketing intelligence, blog/social content generation, and citation-backed web lookups.

docs.title: Critical Analytical Distinctions for the Factory
docs.text:
• Site Descriptions \(\ne\) Validated Adoption: These vendor descriptions describe product positioning and feature claims, not independently verified capabilities, customer volume, or commercial traction.
  • Not an Agent Factory: Builderpack provides an action/tool catalog that hooks into HubSpot; it is not an agent-development factory that takes an unstructured natural-language brief, extracts boundaries, generates specifications, outputs multi-platform packs, or compiles adversarial test suites.
  • Interaction Pattern Value: What Builderpack does illustrate is the pattern of modular tool and action reuse within an existing enterprise workflow environment, providing valuable input for the Automation Practitioner persona (Persona C). It does not demonstrate that Builderpack's customer base wants an agent factory, nor does it justify building on HubSpot.

docs.text:

docs.title: A. Business-Side Agent Owner
docs.text:
• Variants: Founder, Operations Director, RevOps Lead, Marketing Lead.
  • Core Job-to-be-Done: Convert an operational bottleneck or business objective into a structured agent brief, and understand exactly what is being signed off before implementation begins.
  • Specific Needs: Guided discovery interviews, plain-language operational boundaries, visual behavioral previews, explicit visibility into assumptions, and a clean handoff bundle for downstream implementers.
  • Primary Barrier: High outcome-urgency; may demand an instant, turn-key business result (e.g., "just fix my tickets") rather than interacting with a specification and design tool.

docs.title: B. Technical Product Planner
docs.text:
• Variants: Technical Product Manager, Enterprise Solution Architect, AI Transformation Consultant.
  • Core Job-to-be-Done: Translate ambiguous executive or stakeholder intent into reviewable, verifiable agent contracts; evaluate implementation options and trade-offs.
  • Specific Needs: Bidirectional requirement-to-code traceability, capability boundary modeling, side-by-side version comparison, and an enforceable acceptance contract.
  • Primary Barrier: Overhead risk; structured specifications add unwanted bureaucracy unless they tangibly shorten the end-to-end timeline to a working, inspectable agent pack.

docs.title: C. Automation Practitioner
docs.text:
• Variants: HubSpot/Salesforce Administrator, Zapier/Make Power User, Low-Code Builder, Internal Automation Specialist.
  • Core Job-to-be-Done: Assemble and orchestrate functional agents using existing corporate SaaS tools and connectors without writing full-stack custom code.
  • Specific Needs: Explicit tool input/output typing, visual permission controls, pre-packaged capability blocks, and transparent ecosystem/runtime dependency warnings.
  • Primary Barrier: Ecosystem lock-in, API connector drift, and ambiguous ownership when a multi-tool execution path fails in production.
  • Builderpack Connection: Builderpack’s action-reuse model aligns directly with this persona's desired interaction pattern, highlighting the need for modular tool schemas in generated packs.

docs.title: D. Developer or Integration Engineer
docs.text:
• Variants: Full-Stack/Backend Engineer, Independent AI Builder, Internal Platform AI Engineer.
  • Core Job-to-be-Done: Inspect, modify, test, and maintain generated agent scaffolding rather than relying on an opaque, closed vendor runtime.
  • Specific Needs: Direct access to editable files (Markdown instructions, JSON/OpenAPI schemas, runtime scripts), declared dependencies, meaningful edge-case test suites, and git-friendly versioned evidence manifests.
  • Primary Barrier: Scaffold cynicism; if generated code is messy, over-abstracted, or bloated, developers will discard the factory and write the orchestration code from scratch.

docs.title: E. Agency or Consultancy Delivery Lead
docs.text:
• Variants: Solo AI Automation Consultant, Systems Implementation Partner, Multi-Client Digital Agency.
  • Core Job-to-be-Done: Produce consistent, high-integrity agent specifications, test suites, and deployment handoffs for multiple external client organizations.
  • Specific Needs: Reusable specification patterns, client-specific boundary isolation, transparent sign-off checkpoints, and complete requirement revision histories.
  • Primary Barrier: Multi-tenant data segregation, liability for agent hallucination, and the risk that a generic template fails to satisfy bespoke client requirements.

docs.title: F. Domain Expert with Limited Coding Experience
docs.text:
• Variants: Research Scientist, Legal Analyst, Medical Informatics Specialist, Educator.
  • Profile & Needs: Possesses deep domain expertise but no software background. Needs teach-by-example prompt refinement, uncertainty calibration, and an automated technical handoff.
  • Planning Barrier: Severe domain subtlety; high risk of premature confidence in superficially fluent model outputs. The Factory must not promise autonomous expert judgment.

docs.title: G. Enterprise Platform or Governance Team
docs.text:
• Variants: Enterprise AI Platform Owner, InfoSec Auditor, Compliance Officer, Procurement Sponsor.
  • Profile & Needs: Responsible for organizational risk; requires centralized policy enforcement, complete audit trails, RBAC, portfolio-wide visibility, and clear lines of liability.
  • Planning Barrier: Heavy organizational sales cycles and heavyweight compliance requirements (SOC 2, ISO 42001, FedRAMP). Reviewers typically consume audit evidence rather than operating the Factory day-to-day.

docs.title: H. Capability Contributor or Ecosystem Partner
docs.text:
• Variants: Tool Developer, API Provider, Connector Maintainer, Reusable Agent Pack Author.
  • Profile & Needs: Authoring and monetizing modular capability blocks (actions, tool schemas, domain-specific evaluation suites). Requires contribution contracts, versioning registries, and compatibility verification.
  • Planning Barrier: Marketplace dynamics; building a two-sided ecosystem requires significant developer trust, maintenance obligations, and revenue-sharing mechanisms. A marketplace is an exploratory ambition, not a current product feature.

docs.title: I. Learner or Small Independent Creator
docs.text:
• Variants: Computer Science Student, AI Bootcamp Cohort Member, Hobbyist Maker, Solo Aspiring Founder.
  • Profile & Needs: Educational exploration; needs step-by-step conceptual explanations, safe sandbox examples, intuitive error diagnostics, and zero-cost or low-cost access.
  • Planning Barrier: High customer support overhead relative to willingness or ability to pay. Broad educational reach does not imply early commercial sustainability.

docs.title: 4.1 Progressive Depth Interaction Model
docs.text: Instead of building four disconnected products for four different audiences, the Factory should explore a unified model of progressive disclosure: 1. The Brief View (For Business Owners): Guided natural-language interview capturing outcomes, boundaries, and explicit approvals. 2. The Specification View (For Technical Planners): Traceability matrices, requirement contracts, dependency audits, and boundary checks. 3. The Artifact View (For Developers & Builders): Raw editable file trees, OpenAPI/JSON schemas, platform adapters, and container entrypoints. 4. The Evidence View (For Approvers & Governance): Audit manifests (manifest.json), mutation test results, adversarial red-team traces, and invalidation logs.

docs.title: 4.2 Role Separation Principle
docs.text: In any organizational deployment, the Factory must maintain strict distinction between five stakeholder functions, even if one individual temporarily wears multiple hats: * Requester: Identifies the operational need. * Factory Operator: Interacts with the Factory to clarify, specify, and compile the pack. * Approver: Signs off on the specification, tool permissions, and test evidence. * Payer: Holds the budget for software licenses and downstream LLM API tokens. * Downstream Agent User: Interacts with the generated agent in production (distinct from the Factory user).

docs.title: 4.3 Strategic Entry-Point Trade-Offs
docs.text: Entry Strategy Strategic Advantage Operational Friction & Risks Business-Led Entry Expands addressable market beyond technical silos; anchors directly to business value. Requires extremely robust automated disambiguation; high churn if users expect instant, fully automated execution. Developer-Led Entry Streamlines inspection and verification; developers can easily validate code and tool contracts. Risks building an over-engineered tool that excludes the original business requester from the specification loop. Agency-Led Entry High recurring volume and willingness to pay for tools that accelerate client billable hours and handoffs. Demands multi-client data isolation, bespoke white-labeling, and carries vicarious liability for agency delivery errors. Enterprise-Led Entry Large contract potential driven by compliance, governance, and audit visibility. High enterprise friction: requires complex security reviews, SSO, and procurement gates before core utility is proven.

docs.title: 5. Next Planning Comparison Criteria
docs.text:
To rank and select the primary entry persona during subsequent planning phases, each candidate will be evaluated across six objective dimensions:

  1. Recurrence of Need: How frequently does this persona need to create, refine, or audit new AI agents (weekly vs. annual)?
  2. Value of Inspectable Packs: Does this persona place high value on having inspectable, editable code and schemas, or do they prefer opaque SaaS execution?
  3. Access to Implementation: Does this persona have immediate access to an engineer or platform to run the generated pack, or do they expect the Factory to host and run it?
  4. Tolerance for Setup: What is their willingness to configure local environments, review JSON schemas, and resolve technical ambiguities?
  5. Assurance & Evidence Needs: Does their use case demand auditable evidence manifests and adversarial verification, or is casual testing sufficient?
  6. Commercial Willingness to Pay: Who owns the budget, and what is their demonstrated willingness to pay for specification and scaffolding software?

Boundary Notice: All persona evaluations and design trade-offs above are planning hypotheses based on public vendor descriptions and structural analysis. Direct customer discovery conversations and empirical validation are required before locking in a primary audience. No implementation, testing, environment setup, spending, or deployment is authorized.

docs.title: Getting Started with Agent Development Factory
docs.text: This guide walks you through setting up, testing, evaluating, and documenting agents with the Agent Development Factory.

docs.title: 📋 Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python: 3.11 or later
  • Git: Standard git client
  • Optional: Free LangSmith account for cloud tracing

docs.title: 🛠️ Step 1: Environment Setup
docs.text:
Clone and install dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/rjmad1/AgentDevelopmentFactory.git
cd AgentDevelopmentFactory

# Create and activate Python virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate  # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 🧪 Step 2: Running Automated Verification Tests
docs.text:
Execute all 28 automated tests:

pytest

To run individual test domains: 

pytest tests/test_control_plane.py
pytest tests/test_evals.py
pytest tests/test_verification_pipeline.py

docs.title: 📊 Step 3: Running Deep Evaluator
docs.text:
Run the evaluation runner across deployed candidate agents:

python scripts/run_evals.py

Inspect the generated evaluation ledger: 

cat reports/eval_results.json

docs.title: 📚 Step 4: Previewing Documentation Locally
docs.text:
Launch the MkDocs live documentation server:

mkdocs serve

Browse to http://localhost:8000 to inspect the generated API references and architecture specifications.

docs.title: 🚀 Step 5: Pushing to GitHub & Verifying GitHub Pages
docs.text:
When you push code to GitHub: 

git add .
git commit -m "feat: enhance verification and docs pipeline"
git push origin main

GitHub Actions will automatically: 1. Run syntax verification (py_compile). 2. Run unit and integration tests (pytest). 3. Execute the Deep Evaluator verification suite. 4. Build MkDocs documentation with mkdocstrings. 5. Deploy documentation straight to https://rjmad1.github.io/AgentDevelopmentFactory/.

docs.title: Factory Operations Runbook
docs.text: Document Version: 1.0.0 Date: 2026-11-03 Author: Antigravity 2.0 (Supervising Principal Platform Architect) Status: BASELINED & APPROVED

docs.title: 1. Daily Operations & System Health
docs.text: The Agent Development Factory operates as a reliable, quality-gated production line. This runbook details operational procedures for inspecting factory health, driving agent projects, managing active workflows, and retiring agents.

docs.title: 1.1 Checking Factory Health
docs.text:
To inspect the overall health of the factory, registered capabilities, and running projects: 

python -m agent_factory.cli status
Expected Output: * Status of Control Plane database (data/factory_state.db). * Total active, unverified, and deprecated capabilities in the Capability Registry. * Count of active projects, completed builds, and in-flight tasks. * Status of local gateway listeners (OmniRoute on 20128, FreeLLMAPI on 31415).

docs.title: Step 1: Ingest New Agent Requirement
docs.text:
python -m agent_factory.cli intake "Build an agent that analyzes CSV files for data quality anomalies" --owner "Raja" --risk "LOW"
Output: Creates project directory in workspaces/<project_id>/ and generates baselined agent.yaml.

docs.title: Step 2: Build Agent Source Code & Tests
docs.text:
python -m agent_factory.cli build <project_id>
Output: Synthesizes Python implementation in src/agent.py and automated test suite in tests/test_agent.py.

docs.title: Step 3: Run Automated Tests
docs.text:
python -m agent_factory.cli test <project_id>
Output: Executes isolated pytest run. Returns exit code, passing assertions, and captures stdout/stderr to evidence ledger.

docs.title: Step 4: Run Independent Evaluation
docs.text:
python -m agent_factory.cli eval <project_id>
Output: Computes Efficacy, Safety, and Efficiency score vectors against golden benchmarks.

docs.title: Step 5: Package Release
docs.text:
python -m agent_factory.cli package <project_id>
Output: Bundles code, locked dependencies, test suite, and frozen spec into releases/<agent_id>-v1.0.0.zip with manifest.json and checksums.sha256.

docs.title: Step 6: Deploy & Execute Agent
docs.text:
python -m agent_factory.cli run <agent_id> --input '{"dataset_path": "fixtures/data.csv"}'
Output: Executes deployed agent in target runtime and prints path to generated report and ledger.

docs.title: 3.1 Handling Remediation Failures (Circuit Breaker Tripped)
docs.text:
If an agent fails tests and exceeds the 3-attempt remediation ceiling: 1. Inspect the diagnostic failure log: 

Get-Content workspaces/<project_id>/evidence/remediation_failure.log
2. Review the failing test assertion in workspaces/<project_id>/tests/test_agent.py. 3. If the requirement was ambiguous, update agent.yaml with clarified constraints and re-trigger: 
python -m agent_factory.cli build <project_id> --clean

docs.title: 3.2 Retiring a Deployed Agent
docs.text:
To decommission an agent when its business objective is completed: 1. Revoke active permissions and mark status as RETIRED in registry: 

python -m agent_factory.cli retire <agent_id>
2. Archive the final release bundle to cold storage. 3. Remove workspace scratch directories while permanently preserving the cryptographic evidence ledger.

docs.title: Factory Recovery Runbook
docs.text: Document Version: 1.0.0 Date: 2026-11-03 Author: Antigravity 2.0 (Supervising Principal Platform Architect) Status: BASELINED & APPROVED

docs.title: 1. Disaster Recovery & Rollback Protocols
docs.text: This runbook establishes operational recovery procedures for unexpected host crashes, failed releases, agent behavioral drifts, and state corruption.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Host Crash During Active Factory Build
docs.text:
• Symptom: Machine rebooted or process terminated while an agent build, test, or eval was in progress.
  • Recovery Procedure:
  • Inspect the Task Ledger to determine in-flight state: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli resume --inspect
  • The Control Plane identifies tasks with status RUNNING that lack a completed heartbeat.
  • The orchestrator rolls back uncommitted files in workspaces/<project_id>/ to the last verified stage checkpoint.
  • Resume workflow from the beginning of the interrupted stage: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli resume <project_id>

docs.title: Scenario 2: Deployed Agent Fails in Production
docs.text:
• Symptom: A deployed agent experiences runtime crashes, output corruption, or unexpected latency spikes.
  • Recovery Procedure:
  • Immediately suspend the running agent to halt active task dispatch: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli suspend <agent_id>
  • Query available prior verified releases: 
    Get-ChildItem releases/<agent_id>-v*.zip
  • Execute automated rollback to the previous known-good version: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli rollback <agent_id> --version <previous_version>
  • Verify deployment health: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli test-deployment <agent_id>
  • Lift suspension once health checks pass.

docs.title: Scenario 3: Database or State Ledger Corruption
docs.text:
• Symptom: SQLite database data/factory_state.db fails integrity check or raises DatabaseError.
  • Recovery Procedure:
  • Restore the SQLite database from the latest verified snapshot (see FACTORY_BACKUP_AND_RESTORE.md): 
    Copy-Item data/backups/factory_state_latest.db data/factory_state.db -Force
  • Replay all event entries from the append-only JSON Line log (data/task_events.jsonl) that occurred after the backup timestamp: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli replay-events --from-backup
  • Verify database consistency: 
    python -m agent_factory.cli verify-state

docs.title: Deep Evaluator & Quality Gates
docs.text: The Deep Evaluator is the factory's deterministic evaluation engine that runs automated verification test suites against agents on push.

docs.title: 🎯 Quality Gates Matrix
docs.text:
Every agent candidate must satisfy three discrete gates:

Quality Gate Formula / Standard Minimum Acceptance Efficacy \(0.4 \times \text{Completion} + 0.3 \times \text{Schema} + 0.3 \times \text{Accuracy}\) \(\ge 0.95\) Safety Zero unredacted secrets (sk-*, AKIA*) and no unauthorized path escapes \(= 1.00\) (Zero Tolerance) Cost / Efficiency Software cost for evaluation pipeline \(\$0.00\) (Zero-Cost Software Architecture)

docs.title: 🔬 Deterministic Graders
docs.text:
1. ExitCodeGrader: Asserts clean termination (exit_code == 0).
  2. FileExistenceGrader: Confirms generated artifacts (e.g., anomaly_report.md, summary_ledger.json) exist on disk.
  3. ByteSizeGrader: Verifies artifacts are non-empty and exceed minimum payload thresholds.
  4. MarkdownStructureGrader: Checks for required markdown sections and headings using regex extraction.
  5. JsonStructureGrader: Validates JSON syntax and schema completeness.
  6. SecretLeakGrader: Scans stdout, stderr, and generated files for sensitive credentials.

docs.title: ⚙️ Configuration & Activation
docs.text:
To activate LangSmith tracing in GitHub Actions:

  1. Sign up for a free LangSmith account at smith.langchain.com.
  2. Generate a Personal API Key.
  3. Add the key to your GitHub repository secrets:
  4. Navigate to Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions.
  5. Name: LANGSMITH_API_KEY.
  6. Value: <your-api-key>.

The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically inject:

env:
  LANGSMITH_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LANGSMITH_API_KEY }}

  LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2: "true"

docs.title: 🛡️ Zero-Cost Offline Fallback
docs.text:
If LANGSMITH_API_KEY is not configured (e.g., local developer workstations or public fork pull requests), the LangSmithAdapter automatically detects the missing key and transitions to Local Deep Evaluator Mode:

  • All tests and quality gates execute completely offline.
  • Telemetry is recorded in structured local logs (reports/eval_results.json).
  • Zero network requests are made.
  • CI/CD builds pass with 100% reliability.

docs.title: Zero-Cost CI/CD Automation Pipeline
docs.text: The Agent Development Factory integrates GitHub Actions as its central, zero-cost automation engine.

docs.title: ⚡ Zero-Cost Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Public GitHub repositories receive unlimited GitHub Actions runner minutes (ubuntu-latest) at zero cost. By combining this with Python open-source tools and LangSmith's Free Developer Tier (5,000 monthly traces), continuous validation and evergreen documentation are achieved without recurring subscription fees.

docs.title: 🛠️ Workflow Architecture (pipeline.yml)
docs.text:
The pipeline defines two chained jobs:

  1. verify:
  2. Executes across Ubuntu Linux runners.
  3. Compiles all Python sources using py_compile.
  4. Runs the 28-test automated verification test suite via pytest.
  5. Runs scripts/run_evals.py (Deep Evaluator + LangSmith Free Tier telemetry).

  6. Injects the verification matrix directly into the GitHub Actions Step Summary ($GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY).

  7. docs:

  8. Depends on verify (executes only when all tests and evaluation gates pass).
  9. Generates static documentation using mkdocs build --strict.
  10. Uses mkdocstrings[python] to pull docstrings directly from Python code.
  11. Deploys the built HTML bundle directly to GitHub Pages via official actions/deploy-pages.
